root.note: al- is the Arabic article ‘the’. Wiktionary gives the route through Andalusian Arabic.

history: If you rent a flat in Spain, you pay your alquiler in a word from al-Andalus. Arabic kirāʾ meant renting, and with the article it was al-kirāʾ, ‘the renting’. Spanish took article and noun together. The word first settled as alquilé; the final -r came later, as an extra sound with no meaning of its own. The r inside the Arabic word changed too, and became the l of the second syllable. The verb alquilar was then made from the noun. Today the word family covers a tenant's whole life: alquilar, contrato de alquiler, and realquilar, ‘to sublet’.
historyEinfach: Alquiler means ‘rent’. It is an Arabic word. In Arabic, al-kirāʾ means ‘the renting’. Spanish took the two parts, ‘the’ and ‘renting’, as one word. The sounds changed a little over time. The verb alquilar, ‘to rent’, came later from the noun. When you rent a flat, you sign a contrato de alquiler.

elsewhere.text: Arabic speakers may recognise kirāʾ under the Spanish spelling, with the article al- at the front.
